{{Short description|Multiscale analog of homology group}}

In [[persistent homology]], a '''persistent homology group''' is a multiscale analog of a [[Homology (mathematics)|homology group]] that captures information about the evolution of [[Topology|topological features]] across a [[Filtration (mathematics)|filtration]] of spaces. While the ordinary homology group represents nontrivial homology classes of an individual [[topological space]], the persistent homology group tracks only those classes that remain nontrivial across multiple parameters in the underlying filtration. Analogous to the ordinary [[Betti number]], the ranks of the persistent homology groups are known as the [[persistent Betti number]]s. Persistent homology groups were first introduced by [[Herbert Edelsbrunner]], David Letscher, and Afra Zomorodian in a 2002 paper ''Topological Persistence and Simplification'', one of the foundational papers in the fields of persistent homology and [[topological data analysis]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Edelsbrunner |last2=Letscher |last3=Zomorodian |date=2002 |title=Topological Persistence and Simplification |journal=Discrete & Computational Geometry |language=en |volume=28 |issue=4 |pages=511–533 |doi=10.1007/s00454-002-2885-2 |issn=0179-5376|doi-access=free }}</ref>  based largely on the [[persistence barcode]]s and the persistence algorithm, that were first described by Serguei Barannikov in the 1994 paper.<ref name="Barannikov 1994">{{Cite journal|title = Framed Morse complex and its invariants |journal = Advances in Soviet Mathematics  | date = 1994|pages = 93–115|volume = 21|first = Sergey|last = Barannikov |series = ADVSOV |doi=10.1090/advsov/021/03|isbn = 9780821802373 |s2cid = 125829976 |url = https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01745109/file/GeneralizedMorse.pdf }}</ref> Since then, the study of persistent homology groups has led to applications in [[data science]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Chen |first=Li M. |title=Mathematical problems in data science : theoretical and practical methods |date=2015 |others=Zhixun Su, Bo Jiang |isbn=978-3-319-25127-1 |location=Cham |pages=120–124 |oclc=932464024}}</ref> [[machine learning]],<ref>{{Cite book |title=Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction : First IFIP TC 5, WG 8.4, 8.9, 12.9 International Cross-Domain Conference, CD-MAKE 2017, Reggio, Italy, August 29 - September 1, 2017, Proceedings |date=2017 |others=Andreas Holzinger, Peter Kieseberg, A. Min Tjoa, Edgar R. == Definition ==
Let <math>K</math> be a [[simplicial complex]], and let <math>f: K \to \mathbb R</math> be a [[Real-valued function|real-valued]] [[monotonic function]]. Then for some values <math>a_0 < a_1 < \cdots < a_n \in \mathbb R</math> the [[Level set|sublevel-sets]] <math>K(a) := f^{-1}(-\infty, a]</math> yield a sequence of nested subcomplexes <math>\emptyset = K_0 \subseteq K_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq K_n = K</math> known as a ''filtration'' of <math>K</math>.

Applying <math>p^{th}</math> homology to each complex yields a sequence of homology groups <math>0 = H_p (K_0) \to H_p (K_1) \to \cdots \to H_p (K_n) = H_p (K)</math> connected by [[homomorphism]]s induced by the [[inclusion map]]s of the underlying filtration. When homology is taken over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]], we get a sequence of [[vector space]]s and [[linear map]]s known as a [[persistence module]].

Let <math>f_p^{i,j}: H_p (K_i) \to H_p (K_j)</math> be the homomorphism induced by the inclusion <math>K_i \hookrightarrow K_j</math>. Then the <math>p^{th}</math> persistent homology groups are defined as the [[Image (mathematics)|images]] <math>H_p^{i,j} := \operatorname{im} f_p^{i,j}</math> for all <math>1 \leq i \leq j \leq n</math>. In particular, the persistent homology group <math>H_p^{i,i} = H_p (K_i)</math>.

More precisely, the <math>p^{th}</math> persistent homology group can be defined as <math>H_p^{i,j} = Z_p (K_i) / \left( B_p (K_j) \cap Z_p(K_i) \right)</math>, where <math>Z_p(K_\bullet)</math> and <math>B_p(K_\bullet)</math> are the standard p-cycle and p-boundary groups, respectively.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Edelsbrunner |first=Herbert |title=Computational topology : an introduction |date=2010 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |others=J. Harer |isbn=978-0-8218-4925-5 |location=Providence, R.I. |pages=149–153 |oclc=427757156}}</ref>

== Birth and death of homology classes ==
Sometimes the elements of <math>H_p^{i,j}</math> are described as the homology classes that are "born" at or before <math>K_i</math> and that have not yet "died" entering <math>K_j</math>. These notions can be made precise as follows. A homology class <math>\gamma \in H_p (K_i)</math> is said to be ''born'' at <math>K_i</math> if it is not contained in the image of the previous persistent homology group, i.e., <math>\gamma \notin H_p^{i-1, i}</math>. Conversely, <math>\gamma</math> is said to ''die entering'' <math>K_j</math> if <math>\gamma</math> is subsumed (i.e., merges with) another older class as the sequence proceeds from <math>K_{j-1} \to K_j</math>. That is to say, <math>f_p^{i,j-1} (\gamma) \notin H_p^{i-1,j-1}</math> but <math>f_p^{i,j} (\gamma) \in H_p^{i-1,j}</math>. The determination that an older class persists if it merges with a younger class, instead of the other way around, is sometimes known as the ''Elder Rule''.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Progress in information geometry : theory and applications |date=2021 |isbn=978-3-030-65459-7 |editor-last=Nielsen |editor-first=Frank |location=Cham |pages=224 |oclc=1243544872}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Oudot |first=Steve Y. |title=Persistence theory : from quiver representations to data analysis |date=2015 |isbn=978-1-4704-2545-6 |location=Providence, Rhode Island |pages=2–3 |oclc=918149730}}</ref>

The indices <math>i,j</math> at which a homology class <math>\gamma</math> is born and dies entering are known as the ''birth'' and ''death'' indices of <math>\gamma</math>. The difference <math>j-i</math> is known as the ''index persistence'' of <math>\gamma</math>, while the corresponding difference <math>a_j - a_i</math> in function values corresponding to those indices is known as the ''persistence'' of <math>\gamma</math> . If there exists no index at which <math>\gamma</math> dies, it is assigned an infinite death index. Thus, the persistence of each class can be represented as an [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] in the [[Extended real number line|extended real line]] <math>\mathbb R \cup \{\pm \infty\}</math> of either the form <math>[a_i, a_j)</math> or <math>[a_i', \infty)</math>. Since, in the case of an infinite field, the infinite number of classes always have the same persistence,  the collection over ''all'' classes of such intervals does not give meaningful multiplicities  for a [[multiset]] of intervals. Instead, such multiplicities and a multiset of intervals in the extended real line are given by the structure theorem of [[persistent homology|persistence homology]].<ref name="Barannikov 1994" /> This multiset is known as the ''[[persistence barcode]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ghrist |first=Robert |date=2008 |title=Barcodes: The persistent topology of data |url=https://www.ams.org/bull/2008-45-01/S0273-0979-07-01191-3/ |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=61–75 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-07-01191-3 |issn=0273-0979|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Canonical form ==
Concretely, the structure theorem states that for any filtered complex over a field <math>F</math>, there exists a linear transformation that preserves the filtration and converts the filtered complex into so called '''canonical form''', a canonically defined direct sum of filtered complexes of two types: two-dimensional complexes with trivial homology <math>d(e_{a_j})=e_{a_i}</math> and one-dimensional complexes with trivial differential <math>d(e_{a'_i})=0</math>.<ref name="Barannikov 1994"></ref>

== Persistence diagram ==
[[File:Persistence Diagram.png|thumb|An example of a persistence diagram]]
Geometrically, a barcode can be plotted as a multiset of points (with possibly infinite coordinates) <math>(a_i, a_j)</math> in the extended [[Plane (mathematics)|plane]] <math>\left( \mathbb R \cup \{\pm \infty \} \right)^2</math>. By the above definitions, each point will lie above the diagonal, and the distance to the diagonal is exactly equal to the persistence of the corresponding class times <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}</math>.  This construction is known as the ''persistence diagram'', and it provides a way of visualizing the structure of the persistence of homology classes in the sequence of persistent homology groups.<ref name=":0" />
